newsitem.title: USA: Ole Miss buddies prove Nemesis to tobacco companies.
newsitem.headline: Ole Miss buddies prove Nemesis to tobacco companies.

text.p: The nation's $46 billion tobacco industry, armed with legions of lawyers and a seemingly bottomless war chest, has met its match in two southern lawyers from Pascagoula, Miss.

Indeed, when Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore recruited his Ole Miss (University of Mississippi) law school classmate Dick Scruggs to sue the industry in 1994, the suit to recoup the state's costs of treating smokers was seen as little more than a novel twist in a string of failed lawsuits against the industry.
It was easy for tobacco officials to dismiss a pair of lawyers from one of the nation's poorest states. But the industry didn't know the fight it was in for.
Moore, 45, who peppers his southern drawl speech with phrases like "that dog don't hunt," is a former rock musician with the energy of the Everyready battery bunny.

Scruggs, when publicly with Moore, seems almost shy by comparison. But looks are deceiving. The 51-year-old muscular former Navy pilot has never shied away from battle and has made a fortune representing plaintiffs suing asbestos makers.

The two, making countless trips in Scruggs' jet, eventually enlisted four-fifths of the states, prominent plaintiffs lawyers and even Harvard Law School professor Laurence Tribe in the fight against the cigarette makers.

The idea for the Medicaid suits dates to 1993 when Moore was contacted by another former law classmate at the University of Mississippi, Michael Lewis, who practices in Clarksdale, Miss. Lewis was trying to help his secretary's mother, a heavy smoker dying of lung cancer.

The woman was broke after paying medical bills and had turned to Medicaid, the government insurance programme for the poor. This led Lewis to ask Moore if the state could sue the industry to recoup Medicaid funds spent on sick smokers.

Enlisting the help of Scruggs and Harvard's Tribe, Moore filed his landmark suit in May 1994. However, he had to do so without the approval, and even the knowledge, of Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice, a Republican tobacco proponent.

Moore, a Democrat, likes to tell the story of how Fordice reacted to the suit. "He told me it made him want to throw up," Moore said after the case was filed. Fordice filed a suit challenging Moore's authority to bring the case, but the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled the Medicaid suit could stand.
Moore began trying to win over other states, lobbying outside meetings of the National Association of Attorneys General, which has not taken a stand on the suits.

Support was slow at first. Only two other states filed in 1994. But the crusade gained momentum as more whistle-blowers and damaging documents surfaced. The biggest break came when Liggett Group, the smallest of the cigarette makers, decided to settle litigation in March 1996.

The company, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group, negotiated a broader settlement including more states in March 1997 and became the first cigarette maker to admit nicotine is addictive and agreed to turn over documents that could prove damaging to other companies.
A month later the industry contacted Moore and said it wanted to negotiate. Sixteen more states have filed since then, bringing the number of state suits to 40.

The talks have been complex. Not only has it been difficult finding common ground between state and industry officials, but there have been rifts among the states. There were also health groups and plaintiffs lawyers to consider.
Although the talks seemed about to collapse several times, Moore has remained upbeat throughout. One investment adviser described him as "Pollyanna-ish."

But Moore has said all along he had to win. Children's lives could be saved by forcing the industry to change its practices. "This is the most important thing that I will ever accomplish in my life," he said.
